chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Muhammad from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn al-'Aziz who said: One of our companions narrated to me who said:

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) would say, when he raised his head from the last rak'ah of Witr: 'This is the station of one whose good deeds are a favor from You, and his gratitude is weak, and his sin is great, and there is for him nothing but Your gentleness and mercy.'
For indeed You said in Your Book revealed to Your Messenger (peace be upon him and his family): 'They used to sleep little of the night, and in the early morning hours they would seek forgiveness.'

My sleep is long and my standing [in prayer] is short, and this is the dawn hour, and I seek forgiveness from You for my sins with the seeking of forgiveness of one who finds for himself no harm, no benefit, no death, no life, and no resurrection.' Then he would prostrate.
Al-Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: Then he should pray the two rak'ahs of Fajr, up to the point where he says: 'and let him lie down.'

key_terms.الْأَسْحَارِ: The early morning hours before dawn
key_terms.رَكْعَةِ الْوَتْرِ: The last rak'ah of the Witr prayer

ai.seo_question: What is the supplication recited after the Witr prayer according to Imam al-Hasan al-Askari?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Hasan al-Askari (peace be upon him) highlights the spiritual significance of the Witr prayer as a moment of humble self-accounting, where the Imam contrasts his limited gratitude with the vastness of his sins, relying solely on divine mercy. By citing the verse regarding those who pray in the last part of the night, the Imam emphasizes the virtue of *Tahajjud* and *Istighfar* (seeking forgiveness) during the *Sahar* (pre-dawn) hours. The inclusion of the juristic note regarding the Fajr prayer underscores the continuity of worship, linking the voluntary night prayer with the obligatory dawn prayer in the daily rhythm of a believer's devotion.
